jsnvu6-e180490-d1e106.summary: Rubric for Question 6: whether faith is a virtuous habit, referring to Aquinas.

jsnvu6-e180490-d1e115.summary: Argument that faith is not a virtue: the virtues were in Christ most fully, but Christ, a comprehensor, did not have faith.
claims: Christ lacked faith yet had all virtues, so faith is not a virtue (objection)

jsnvu6-e180490-d1e128.summary: Second argument: faith would be either acquired or infused. Not acquired, since philosophers, who treat acquired virtues adequately, do not count it; not infused, since faith comes by hearing (Rom. 10). Even if infused, it would not be virtuous, since acquired faith is not counted among acquired virtues and infused faith should relate to infused virtues similarly.
claims: Faith is neither an acquired nor an infused virtue (objection)
Faith comes by hearing and so seems not infused (objection)

jsnvu6-e180490-d1e155.summary: Argument for the opposite: every intellectual habit that always speaks truly is a virtue (Ethics VI), and nothing false can fall under faith, as will be shown.
claims: Faith is a virtue because it is an intellectual habit that never assents to falsehood

jsnvu6-e180490-d1e166.summary: Second argument for the opposite: faith is listed with charity among infused habits, and charity is a virtue.
claims: Faith, numbered with charity, is a virtue

jsnvu6-e180490-d1e175.summary: Outline of the response: whether faith is a virtuous habit; whether it is infused; and its order to hope and charity.

jsnvu6-e180490-d1e188.summary: First article: 'virtue' is taken broadly, for any laudable habit inclining a power to a good act, or strictly, for a habit bringing a power to the ultimate perfection due its act. Broadly, faith is a virtue, inclining the intellect to assent to supernatural truth necessary for salvation, which adds a new aspect of good beyond truth. Strictly, faith is not a virtue, since a proper intellectual virtue perfects the intellect to behold its object in itself or by resolution to what is seen in itself, which faith does not do.
claims: Faith is a virtue in the broad sense of a laudable habit inclining to a good act
Faith is not a virtue in the strict sense, since it does not make the intellect see its object in itself or by resolution to evident principles
Assent to truth necessary for salvation adds a distinct aspect of good
concepts: broad vs. strict sense of virtue

jsnvu6-e180490-d1e247.summary: In either sense, faith is no more or less a virtue with or without charity in the will: its act of assenting to supernatural truth is no more perfect cognitively when charity is present; charity adds only the extrinsic perfection of merit. Faith and charity are not like prudence and moral virtue, which are acquired together and perfect each other's acts; faith depends on charity neither in habit, being naturally prior, nor in act. Though the will inclines the intellect to believe, it need not be informed by charity.
claims: Faith is equally a virtue with or without charity
Charity adds to faith's act only the extrinsic perfection of merit
Unlike prudence and moral virtue, faith does not depend on charity for its perfection
The will moves the intellect to believe without needing to be informed by charity

jsnvu6-e180490-d1e304.summary: Second article: faith is an infused habit. From Scripture: Eph. 2 calls it God's gift; Heb. 11 says without faith one cannot please God, yet baptized infants with no acquired habit please him; and charity, with which faith is numbered, is poured out by the Spirit (Rom. 5). By probable argument: what orders us immediately to a supernatural end comes immediately from a supernatural agent, since end and agent correspond. Faith is infused not because without it we could not believe supernatural truth, but because we could not do so as promptly and easily (Book 2, d.28).
claims: Faith is an infused habit
What orders immediately to a supernatural end is from a supernatural agent
Infused faith is not strictly necessary for believing but for believing promptly and easily

jsnvu6-e180490-d1e349.summary: Third article: in order of time faith, hope, and charity are infused together, since God, not failing in necessities, does not infuse one without the others, which are insufficient alone (given the recipient's disposition). In order of nature faith precedes: acts of hoping and loving presuppose believing, since affection presupposes cognition; and Heb. 11 calls faith the substance, i.e. foundation, of things hoped for, and states that whoever approaches God must believe.
claims: Faith, hope, and charity are infused simultaneously in time
Faith is naturally prior to hope and charity
Affection for the good presupposes cognition of it

jsnvu6-e180490-d1e391.summary: Reply to the first objection: virtues implying no imperfection in their act were most fully in Christ; but faith, needed only in the state of meriting, implies imperfection since it is of the unseen, so it was not in Christ, who saw God's essence from the instant of conception.
claims: Faith implies imperfection because it concerns the unseen
Christ lacked faith because he saw God from conception

jsnvu6-e180490-d1e413.summary: Reply to the second objection: faith is an infused virtue in the broad, not the philosophers' strict, sense. That faith comes by hearing is true regarding the proposal of credibles, not the habit: given the habit, the credibles must be proposed for it to issue in act.
claims: Faith is an infused virtue only in the broad sense
Hearing supplies the proposal of credibles, not the habit itself

jsnvu6-e180490-d1e433.summary: Reply to the first argument for the opposite: not every truth-speaking habit is a virtue strictly, but only one by which truth is perfectly known through evidence in itself or by resolution to self-evident principles, which faith lacks.
claims: Only habits giving evident knowledge are intellectual virtues strictly

jsnvu6-e180490-d1e449.summary: Reply to the second: faith and charity differ because love can be perfect where cognition is imperfect. Love's intensity tracks the goodness of what is known, not the certainty of the knowing: we love more a greater good known probably than a lesser good known certainly. Since faith gives obscure knowledge of the most perfect good, charity's act can be perfect and its habit a strict virtue though faith, eliciting an imperfect act, is not strictly a virtue.
claims: Love can be perfect even when cognition of its object is imperfect
The intensity of love follows the estimated goodness of the object, not the certainty of knowledge
Charity can be a strict virtue though faith is not

jsnvu6-e180490.summary: Question 6 asks whether faith is a virtuous habit, answering in three articles. (1) Distinguishing virtue broadly (any laudable habit inclining to good acts) from strictly (a habit bringing a power to its ultimate due perfection), Durandus holds that faith is a virtue only broadly: it inclines the intellect to supernatural truth necessary for salvation, but does not let it behold its object in itself or by resolution to evident principles. Faith is equally virtuous with or without charity, since charity adds only the extrinsic perfection of merit; it does not stand to charity as prudence stands to moral virtue. (2) Faith is infused, as Scripture, infant baptism, and the correspondence of supernatural end and agent show; yet it is infused so that we may believe promptly and easily, not because believing is otherwise impossible. (3) Faith, hope, and charity are infused at the same time, but faith is prior in nature, since affection presupposes cognition. In the replies, Christ lacked faith because he saw God from conception; hearing supplies the proposal of credibles, not the habit; and charity can be a strict virtue despite faith's imperfection, because love follows the estimated goodness of its object rather than the certainty of knowing it.
claims: Faith is a virtue only in a broad, not strict, sense
Faith's virtue-status is unaffected by the presence of charity
Faith is an infused habit, infused for promptness and ease of belief
Faith, hope, and charity are infused simultaneously, faith being naturally prior
Christ did not have faith
Charity can be strictly a virtue though faith's cognition is imperfect
